en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on Silk (Kosiyavagga) 12.
The Training Rule on Pure Black [Silk].
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks had blankets made from pure black sheep’s wool.
People, while wandering on a tour of the monastery, saw them and complained, grumbled, and spread it about:
“How can these recluses, sons of the Sakyans, have blankets made from pure black sheep’s wool? They are just like householders who indulge in worldly pleasures!”
The monks heard those people grumbling, complaining, and criticizing.
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so forth]... they grumbled, complained, and criticized:
"How can the group-of-six monks have a rug made from pure black wool?"
Then those monks, having rebuked the group-of-six monks in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“… ‘Is it true, monks, that you have had a rug made from pure black wool?
‘It is true, Blessed One.’”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can you, foolish men, have a rug made from pure black wool?
This, foolish men, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence…” [and so on].
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:
“Whosoever, however, a monk should have a rug made of pure black sheep’s wool, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
Whosoever, however...
Whoever is such a one … [as described] … “a bhikkhu” … this is what is intended by the term “bhikkhu” in this context.
"Black" means two kinds of black:
either black by birth or black by dye.
"Spread out" means it has been made by spreading [the material], not by weaving. "Should have it made" means...
Whether he makes it himself or causes it to be made, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the act of undertaking.
Upon acquisition, it becomes subject to relinquishment (*nissaggiya*).
It must be relinquished to the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual.
And furthermore, monks, it should be relinquished in this way:
“… ‘Venerable sir, this rug made of pure black woolen sheep’s wool which I had made is to be relinquished.’”
“I relinquish this to the Saṅgha. … “One should give it” … “They should give it” … [and so on].
"I give it to the Venerable One.
If one completes by oneself what was begun by oneself, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If one has others complete what was begun by oneself, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If she has it finished by herself after others have begun it, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If she has it finished by others after others have begun it, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If she makes it or has it made for the sake of another, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one obtains and uses something made by another, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
There is no offense if one makes a canopy, a floor-covering, a screen-wall, a mattress, or a pillow.
"In the case of one who is insane,
and in the case of the first offender.
The second training rule on the purely black [offense] is concluded.
